title: The temple as a model of the world
eyebrow: Why the temple looks the way it does
dek: An Egyptian temple was a house for a god. It was also a model of the world at the moment it was created. Once you know the story, the gateways, courts, column halls and dark inner rooms of Karnak start to make sense.

creation.heading: The story the building retells
creation.intro: Egyptian priests told several creation stories. The one that explains temple design best goes like this. Step through it.

steps.label: Nothing but water
steps.text: Before anything existed there was only [[nun]]: a dark, endless ocean of nothingness. No land, no sky, no light.

steps.label: The sleeping creator
steps.text: The creator, the sun god [[atum]], drifted asleep in this water for longer than anyone could count.

steps.label: The first land
steps.text: Atum woke up and made a small island rise out of the water. This was the [[primeval-mound]], the first dry ground, the site of the very first event. Standing on it, he began to create everything else.

steps.label: Air and moisture
steps.text: His first children were [[shu]], the air, and [[tefnut]], moisture.

steps.label: Earth and sky
steps.text: Their children were [[geb]], the earth, and [[nut]], the sky. More generations followed until every part of nature existed, each with its own god in charge.

citations.locator: Creation from Nun; Atum; the mound of the First Event; Shu, Tefnut, Geb and Nut

temple.heading: Walk into the past
temple.intro: A temple rebuilt that first moment in stone. The holy rooms at the back stood for the mound. Everything in front of them was the world around it. Walk from the gate to the sanctuary and three things change at once.

steps.label: The gateway
steps.text: Two massive towers with a door between them: the [[pylon]]. It stands for the horizon, the edge of the world, where the sun appears each morning. You enter the god’s world through it.

steps.label: The open court
steps.text: No roof at all. Full sunlight, and the floor is at its lowest point. This is the present-day, ordinary world, as far from the first moment as you can be inside the walls.

steps.label: The hypostyle hall
steps.text: A roof again, carried on columns shaped like papyrus plants. Light comes only through high stone window grilles (the [[clerestory]]). In the model, a [[hypostyle]] hall is the papyrus thicket that grew in the swampy ground at the edge of the first mound. The floor has risen a little; the ceiling has come down.

steps.label: The holy of holies
steps.text: The [[holy-of-holies]]: small, enclosed and almost dark. The floor is at its highest, the ceiling at its lowest. A single small shaft of light fell on the god’s [[cult-statue]]. This room stood for the mound itself, the place where creation began. Only the king and a few priests ever went in.

temple.summary: So, walking inward, you climb, the ceiling comes down and the light fades. You are walking backwards in time, from the bright everyday world to the dark, wet first moment, when the god stood on dry land for the first time.

citations.locator: Temples as replicas of the early universe; rising floor, lowering ceiling, decreasing light; restricted access; hypostyle as papyrus thicket

sections.heading: The gateway is the horizon
text: Look at the hieroglyph [[akhet]], “horizon”: the sun sitting between two hills. It marks the place where the sun rises and sets.

Now look at a [[pylon]] from the front: two sloping towers with a lower doorway between them. It is the same outline, at the size of a building. So a temple gateway is more than a wall to keep people out. It is the horizon in stone, the place where the sun is reborn every morning, and every time you walk through one you cross the edge of the world.

citations.locator: Egyptian architecture: pylon and the akhet hieroglyph (citing Wilkinson 2005, p. 195)

sections.heading: Who saw all this?
text: Very few people. The dim, closed rooms at the back were meant to carry whoever entered back to the beginning of time, and that privilege belonged to the king and a small number of priests. Most Egyptians never saw the sanctuary.
When ordinary people did come close to the god, it was usually at festivals, when the statue was carried out of the temple in its portable boat shrine (a [[bark]]).

citations.locator: Restricted access to the holy of holies

karnak.heading: Now find it at Karnak
text: Karnak follows the pattern, but not tidily, because it was not built in one go. Senusret I built a limestone temple here in the 1900s BC. For more than 1,500 years after that, kings kept adding gateways, courts and halls in front of it, mostly on the west side, towards the Nile. The newest gateway ended up on the outside and the oldest shrine deep inside.

So at Karnak you walk into the past twice. In the model, you walk back to the first moment of the world. In the stonework, you walk back through the temple’s own history: roughly speaking, each gateway you pass is older than the one before.

figure.caption: Karnak from the air, looking north. The Nile is at the top left. The main line of the temple runs from the entrance on the left (west) to the oldest parts on the right (east). The numbers match the list below.

parts.label: First Pylon
parts.text: The entrance you use today. It is the outermost gateway and the newest: begun under Nectanebo I in the 300s BC and never finished.

parts.label: Great Court
parts.role: The open court: the everyday world
parts.text: No roof, full sun. Rows of papyrus-bud columns line the north and south sides.

parts.label: Great Hypostyle Hall
parts.text: 134 stone papyrus plants: open flowers on the twelve tall columns of the central aisle, closed buds on the 122 others. The ruin is bright because the roof has fallen. With the roof on it was dim, lit from the high window grilles: a marsh at dusk, between the sunlit court and the dark sanctuary.

parts.label: Third to Sixth Pylons
parts.text: Four more gateways close together, with narrow halls and courts between them. The standing obelisks are here. The Fourth and Fifth Pylons, built by Thutmose I, are the oldest parts of the temple still standing in place.

parts.label: Sanctuary and the “Middle Kingdom court”
parts.text: The granite shrine in the centre was built in the name of Philip III Arrhidaeus for the god’s portable [[bark]]. Behind it is a wide, almost empty square. Senusret I’s temple stood there, with the shrine that held the statue of Amun-Ra: the heart of the cult. Hardly anything is left of it; the oldest and holiest place at Karnak is now open ground.

parts.label: Akhmenu
parts.text: The temple does not stop at the sanctuary. Thutmose III added a large festival hall behind it, and its layout echoed Senusret I’s old temple. The textbook pattern has no place for a building here. Karnak grew at both ends.

parts.label: Sacred Lake
parts.text: Thutmose III records digging a lake here. Temple lakes stood for [[nun]], the water the world rose out of, and supplied water for the priests’ purification.

parts.label: Southern gateways
parts.text: A textbook temple has one line of gateways. Karnak has two: the Seventh to Tenth Pylons run south from the main temple. The photo shows the Eighth Pylon, built by Hatshepsut.

parts.label: Enclosure wall
parts.role: The edge of the god’s world
parts.text: The huge mud-brick wall around the whole precinct, also built under Nectanebo I. Everything inside it belonged to the god.

karnak.closing: As we add the other halls and temples of Karnak to this guide, each one will say where it sits in this model.
